awd_titl_txt: Conference: 10th Lake Michigan Workshop on Combinatorics and Graph Theory
awd_abstract_narration:
The 10th Lake Michigan Workshop on Combinatorics and Graph Theory will be held at the University of Illinois Chicago on April 5–6, 2025. The workshop will benefit graduate students and junior researchers in multiple subfields of discrete mathematics, working at institutions in the Great Lakes area and beyond. It is built around two sets of three tutorial lectures, focusing on state-of-the-art techniques and results on which the speakers are particularly qualified to expound. There will also be short talks by students and early-career researchers. There will be ample unscheduled time during the weekend, allowing new research collaborations to commence and active collaborations to be continued. Junior participants will establish valuable connections with more senior colleagues and receive guidance from them in a relaxed and informal environment.

Combinatorics and graph theory are two very active areas of research within the broader field of discrete mathematics, with important ties to disciplines such as statistical physics, probability theory, and computer science. In the immediate vicinity of Lake Michigan there are a large number of researchers and students working on a variety of graph theoretical and combinatorial problems. This workshop will bring many of these scholars together. Through the tutorial lectures, short talks, and informal collaboration time, the workshop will train early-career researchers in important and emerging techniques of combinatorics and graph theory. The tutorial speakers for the 2024 workshop are confirmed to be Rose McCarty (Georgia Institute of Technology), Greta Panova (University of Southern California), and Mehtaab Sawhney (Columbia University). The PIs have selected tutorial speakers with the explicit goal of representing disparate subfields of combinatorics and graph theory, with McCarty as an expert in structural graph theory, Panova an expert in algebraic combinatorics, and Sawhney an expert in additive, extremal, and probabilistic combinatorics. The website for the workshop is https://marcusmichelen.org/LakeMichiganWorkshop2025.php

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The 10th Lake Michigan Workshop on Combinatorics and Graph Theory (LMWCGT) was held at the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC) to advance research and foster collaboration within the discrete mathematics community in the Great Lakes region. The workshop brought together approximately 80 participants, including leading faculty, postdoctoral researchers, and a significant number of graduate students.

Intellectual Merit

The primary scientific objective of the workshop was to explore the frontiers of combinatorics and graph theory—fields that study the properties of discrete structures and their connections to algebra, probability, and computer science. The program featured three distinguished speakers who delivered multi-part tutorials on cutting-edge topics:

(1) Hypercontractivity and Additive Combinatorics (Prof. Mehtaab Sawhney, Columbia University): Discussing advanced probabilistic tools used to analyze sparse functions and applications to additive number theory. 

    (2) Structural Graph Theory and Logic (Prof. Rose McCarty, Georgia Tech): Exploring how the complexity of large graphs can be classified using mathematical logic.

    (3) Algebraic Combinatorics and Computational Complexity (Prof. Great Panova, University of Southern California): Investigating how counting mathematical objects can help answer fundamental questions in computer science, such as the relationship between P and NP.

In addition, there were two shorter talks:

  1. Spanning Trees and Continued Fractions (Prof. Swee Hong Chan, Rutgers University): Proving new results on spanning trees using number theory.

2. Sublinear expander and applications (Prof. Abhishek Methuku, University of Illinois Urbana Champaign): Discussing sublinear expanders and their applications to some longstanding problems in graph theory. 

These sessions provided a rigorous environment for participants to learn new techniques and discuss open problems, directly contributing to the advancement of mathematical knowledge and bridging distinct mathematical sub-disciplines.

Broader Impacts

The project achieved significant impact through the development of human resources and the strengthening of the regional scientific infrastructure:

  • Early-Career Development: A substantial portion of the award was used to provide travel and lodging support for graduate students. This allowed junior researchers to engage directly with leaders in the field, facilitating mentorship that is critical for their professional transition into academia or industry.
  • Regional Synergy: The workshop solidified the "Lake Michigan" research corridor by connecting institutions across Illinois, Indiana, and Michigan. This regional focus encourages long-term collaborative research projects that persist well beyond the duration of the event.

In summary, the 10th LMWCGT successfully combined high-level mathematical instruction with professional networking, reinforcing the Midwest's position as a hub for innovation in discrete mathematics.
